items.stem: At CSSD, DDH (District Data Hub) is the destination for inbound syncs like Sync-SRC-DDH — but many syncs export data out of DDH (e.g. Sync-DDH-AAD, which pushes to Azure AD / Entra). In those outbound syncs, what role does DDH play?

options.text: Source — data flows DDH → the other system
Destination — DDH is always the destination
Neither — DDH is only a hub, never a source or destination
Both source and destination within that one sync

items.explanation: Source vs destination is set per sync by the direction of flow, not fixed to a system. DDH is the destination for inbound syncs (Sync-SRC-DDH) and the source for outbound syncs (Sync-DDH-AAD → Azure AD/Entra, Sync-DDH-SPO → SharePoint). The Sync-<source>-<destination> naming convention names each end.

misconceptions.b: DDH is the destination only for inbound syncs. In Sync-DDH-AAD the data originates in DDH and lands in Azure AD, so DDH is the source there.
misconceptions.c: Every sync has a concrete source and destination; calling DDH a 'hub' just means it plays both roles across different syncs.
misconceptions.d: A single sync is one-directional — DDH is the source or the destination for a given sync, never both at once.

items.stem: In the inbound Sync-SRC-DDH integration (data flowing into the DDH), classify each system as Source or Destination: (1) PowerSchool, (2) DDH, (3) HRAD, (4) ServiceNow.
items.sampleAnswer: In Sync-SRC-DDH the DDH is the destination and PowerSchool, HRAD, and ServiceNow are the sources feeding it. (The roles are per-sync: in an outbound sync like Sync-DDH-AAD the DDH is instead the source.)

items.stem: What defines a system as the "source" in a sync?

options.text: It is the largest or most important system
It is where the data originates / is maintained (the system of record)
It is the system Synnduit writes the final data into
It is whichever system runs on SQL Server

items.explanation: The source is the system of record — where the data is authored and maintained — regardless of size or importance.

misconceptions.a: Importance is irrelevant; HR is the source for staff because it authors that data, even though DDH is the district hub.
misconceptions.d: The underlying database technology does not determine the role.

items.stem: Employee records are authored and maintained in HR, then kept in sync into the DDH. In Synnduit terms, HR is the ___ and DDH is the ___.

options.text: destination; source
source; destination
source; source
destination; destination

items.explanation: Data originates in HR (source) and lands in the DDH (destination). Flow is always source → destination.

misconceptions.a: This inverts the flow — data does not originate in the DDH.

items.stem: Which direction does data flow in a Synnduit sync?

options.text: Destination → Source
Source → Destination
Both directions at once
Whichever direction has fewer records

items.explanation: Synnduit reads a snapshot from the source and applies changes to the destination: source → destination.

misconceptions.c: A single sync is one-directional; bidirectional behavior would be two separate syncs.

items.stem: The Sync-DDH-AD integration runs two syncs back to back: first DDH → Active Directory, then Active Directory → HRAD. What role does on-prem Active Directory play across these two syncs?

options.text: Destination in the first (DDH → AD), then source in the second (AD → HRAD)
Source in both syncs
Destination in both syncs
No role — DDH syncs directly to HRAD in one step

items.explanation: Roles are per-sync. In DDH → AD, Active Directory is the destination; in AD → HRAD, that same Active Directory is the source. Sync-DDH-AD bundles both, run separately back to back, so data hops DDH → AD → HRAD — the same per-sync role rule that makes DDH itself a hub.

misconceptions.b: AD only receives data in the first sync (DDH → AD); it isn't the source there.
misconceptions.c: In the second sync (AD → HRAD) AD is the source, not the destination.
misconceptions.d: There is no direct DDH → HRAD sync here; the data passes through AD in two separate one-directional syncs.
